title: Linked List Cycle
prompt:
Given a linked list, determine whether it contains a cycle, where some node's `next` pointer eventually points back to an earlier node in the list instead of `null`.

Since a JSON test case can't represent an actual cyclic pointer structure, the list is encoded as `[values, pos]`: `values` is the array of node values in order, and `pos` is the zero-based index of the node that the last node's `next` pointer connects back to (forming a cycle at that node), or `-1` if there is no cycle at all. For example, `values = [3,2,0,-4], pos = 1` means the list is `3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4 -> (back to node at index 1, i.e. the node with value 2)`. Your function should build the real linked structure (with the cycle, if any) internally from this encoding, then determine whether a cycle exists and return `True` or `False`.

examples.explanation: There is a cycle: the tail connects back to the node at index 1 (value 2).
The tail connects back to the head, forming a cycle.
No cycle; the single node's next is null.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 10^4]
pos is -1 or a valid index into values
hints: Detecting a cycle without extra memory means you can't just store every node you've visited in a set (well, you could, but there's a more elegant O(1)-space trick).
Floyd's cycle detection: use two pointers, one moving one step at a time and one moving two steps at a time.
If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer and they will point to the exact same node. If the fast pointer reaches null first, there is no cycle.

solution.approach: Build the actual linked list from the values array, then, if pos is not -1, connect the last node's next pointer to the node at index pos to form a real cycle. Run Floyd's tortoise-and-hare: a slow pointer advances one node at a time, a fast pointer advances two nodes at a time. If they ever meet (same node reference), a cycle exists. If the fast pointer reaches null (or its next is null), there is no cycle.
